title: Epidemiology and Population Health
answer: Syndromic surveillance, outbreak mapping, vaccine waning, social determinants and scarce resource allocation.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: Syndromic Surveillance
children.blurb: Syndromic surveillance is the practice of monitoring health data that arrives before a diagnosis is confirmed, such as emergency department chief complaints, over-the-counter medicine sales, school absenteeism, calls to nurse hotlines, and search or social media activity.

children.name: Outbreak Mapping
children.blurb: Outbreak mapping is the work of turning case reports, laboratory results and syndromic signals into a picture of where a disease is, how fast it is moving and who is at risk.

children.name: Vaccine Waning Models
children.blurb: Vaccine waning models estimate how protection from a vaccine declines over time, both against infection and against severe outcomes such as hospitalisation and death.

children.name: Social Determinants of Health
children.blurb: Social determinants of health are the conditions in which people are born, grow, live, work and age, including income, housing, education, employment, food access, transportation and neighborhood safety.

children.name: Allocating Scarce Resources
children.blurb: Allocating scarce resources in epidemiology and population health means deciding who receives limited things: intensive care beds, vaccines, ventilators, screening slots, dialysis time, and clinical staff hours.

sections.body: Epidemiology and population health is the study of how disease moves through groups of people rather than through one patient at a time, and AI is now doing real work at that scale. Syndromic surveillance systems scan emergency department complaints, over the counter drug sales, school absence records and search queries for early signs that something is spreading, often before lab confirmation arrives. Outbreak mapping combines case reports with mobility data and genomic sequences to reconstruct where a pathogen has been and where it is going. Vaccine waning models estimate how protection decays over time and how that decay interacts with new variants and booster timing. Social determinants work uses routinely collected data on housing, income and access to care to explain why the same pathogen produces different outcomes in different neighborhoods. Allocation work applies optimization and fairness criteria to decisions about who receives a limited supply of beds, antivirals or vaccines.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The strongest results are in detection and situational awareness. Surveillance signals and genomic outbreak reconstruction now routinely inform public health decisions, and the statistical machinery behind them is well understood. The harder problems are causal and normative. Vaccine waning estimates depend on assumptions about exposure, prior infection and reporting that are difficult to verify, and models can disagree sharply when those assumptions shift. Social determinants models often capture correlation and can encode the very inequities they aim to describe if the underlying data reflect unequal access to care. Allocation algorithms can produce defensible rankings, but the choice of objective, whether to prioritize lives saved, life years, or equity, is a value judgment that no model resolves. The honest limit across all of this is that population data are messy, delayed and incomplete, and a confident looking map can hide substantial uncertainty.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages here move from watching to explaining to deciding. Syndromic Surveillance covers the earliest signal layer, the everyday data streams that flag unusual activity before diagnoses are confirmed. Outbreak Mapping takes those signals and case data and turns them into a spatial and genomic picture of spread. Vaccine Waning Models sit alongside it, addressing the changing susceptibility of a population over time rather than the location of cases. Social Determinants of Health asks why the burden falls unevenly and what structural factors drive the pattern. Allocating Scarce Resources is the endpoint, where all of the above feeds into decisions about who gets treated when supply runs short. A reader new to the field would start with surveillance and mapping for the mechanics, then move to waning and social determinants for the context, and finish with allocation for the applied and ethical questions.
